I appreciate the increased level of detail on a per-model level, but I am also a bit suspicious, since prompt caching also requires data retention. I do not believe that all providers are implementing privacy-preserving caching (e.g. build a prefix tree based on partial hashes of the conversation and encrypt the KV cache with a key derived from the conversation or provided by the client), so a note about maximum cache duration should be included.

My setup:

Windows 11
VS Code Remote-SSH
Ubuntu Server 26.04
OpenCode running on the remote host
Supabase MCP

This also affects Vercel MCP.

VS Code port forwarding does not fully solve the issue because OpenCode uses dynamic callback ports.

A device authorization flow or a paste-code fallback would make OpenCode usable in Remote-SSH environments.

Closing this because the shell-tool architecture has moved substantially and #39567 added parser-based permission handling, so this branch is no longer the right shape to merge.

One distinction worth preserving for future work: `ShellParse.scan` currently extracts command permission resources and directory arguments for commands such as `cd`, while #39567 intentionally kept external-directory checks limited to the working directory. The argument-level advisory this PR implemented therefore remains uncovered. In particular, it detected external paths in:

- redirect targets such as `echo hi >/outside/out.txt`
- assignment values such as `FOO=/outside/x cat y`
- parameter defaults such as `cat ${FILE:-/outside/x}`
- escaped or partly quoted paths such as `/outside/my\ dir/file` and `/outside/"my dir"/file`

It also avoided treating paths that appear only in comments or heredoc bodies as references. That is a different concern from splitting commands for permission approval. If this coverage becomes useful later, the clean implementation now would be to extend `ShellParse`'s canonical result rather than add unbash alongside it as a second parser.

Closing this to avoid keeping a stale and conflicting implementation open.

This request would also directly prevent a class of correctness bugs I hit with concurrent sessions. Posting here rather than opening a duplicate issue, since this is the same root cause.

Real-world failure caused by the missing env var
I ran two opencode sessions in parallel, one per project directory (proj-a/ and proj-b/). Both agents created a temporary helper script with the same generic name (gen_appendix.py) in the shared pre-approved temp directory (%TEMP%\opencode).

Because there is no session identifier available in the subprocess environment, the agent could not name its scratch file uniquely. Session B overwrote the file while session A was still using it; session A then executed session B's script content (different paths, different logic) and wrote its output into the wrong project directory. The corruption was only caught because the script happened to print the output path.

Why this matters beyond external-tool correlation
The issue body frames OPENCODE_SESSION_ID as a need for external tooling (logging, orchestration). My case shows the env var is also needed for agent-internal correctness: an agent cannot isolate its own scratch files across concurrent sessions without it. That makes this a reliability/feature-availability gap, not just an observability nicety.

Concrete benefit if implemented
Agents could name temp files as ${OPENCODE_SESSION_ID}_<name> (or use a session-scoped dir such as %TEMP%\opencode\<session-id>\), eliminating last-writer-wins collisions entirely. This matches the project's own pattern of unique names in the tool-output store (e.g. tool_<random>).

Happy to provide more details or test once implemented.

+1 — same root cause here, with additional findings that may help the team narrow it down.

## New findings

1. **Both GitHub and Google OAuth providers fail with the same 500.** Not provider-specific.
2. **`error_description` in the callback URL leaks SQL fragments and the user's real email.** This is a security concern — see details below.

## Reproduction steps (verified)

1. Open https://opencode.ai/auth in a clean browser profile (no extensions, no existing cookies)
2. Click "Continue with GitHub" (or "Continue with Google")
3. Complete the OAuth flow on the provider side
4. Provider redirects back to `https://auth.opencode.ai/{github|google}/callback?code=...&state=...`
5. Server returns `500 Internal Server Error`
6. Browser is then redirected to `https://opencode.ai/auth/callback?error=server_error&error_description=...`

## Evidence — `error_description` leaks SQL + email

**GitHub login** — `error_description` contains:
```
Failed query: insert into account ... params: acc_01KZ3AFQ...  (email field empty)
```
GitHub `/user` API does not return private email (only public email), so `email` arrives empty at the backend and the INSERT fails.

**Google login** — `error_description` contains the same SQL fragment, but this time **with the user's real email embedded**:
```
... insert into account ... <REDACTED_USER_EMAIL> ...
```
i.e. the backend takes the same code path even when email is present, so the bug is NOT "email is empty" — it is the INSERT itself failing in both cases.

**Security note:** returning raw SQL + PII (user email) in a URL query parameter to the browser is a data leak. The `error_description` should be sanitized before being reflected to the client.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- Network: verified through a US proxy (Clash, node `🇺🇸 US 01`) — `curl -I https://opencode.ai/auth` returns 302, `https://auth.opencode.ai/github/authorize` returns 302 to GitHub. Confirmed not a network/DNS/cert issue.
- Browser: reproduced in both Edge and Chrome, including an extension-free InPrivate window.
- System clock: accurate (verified against NTP).
- Hosts file: clean (no `opencode` entries).

## Related issues

- #40236 — same 500 after Go subscription
- #39153 — same 500 when fetching Go API key

These three look like the same backend `INSERT into account` failure surfacing at different points in the flow (login / subscription / key issuance). Hope this helps — happy to provide more traces if needed.

Follow-up before I write anything, because a local check changed my read of the two directions.

The current behavior is not just incidental, it is pinned by an existing test: `packages/core/test/session-runner-message.test.ts:330`, "drops provider-native continuation metadata from failed assistant turns". It asserts that an errored turn replays `reasoning` with `providerMetadata: undefined` *and* keeps the `tool-call` / `tool-result` parts. So that test encodes exactly the shape this issue says Anthropic rejects.

Baseline on `dev`: 6 pass in that file.

That means either direction has to touch that test, which makes the choice less about the fix site and more about which invariant you want asserted:

- Relaxing the `message.error === undefined` guard means the test's premise changes: errored turns would keep signed/redacted thinking when provider+model match. The test would assert reuse instead of dropping.
- Dropping the errored turn's `tool-call` parts keeps the "no provider state reused" property the test is protecting, and instead removes the orphaned `tool_use`. The test's reasoning assertion stays as-is; its tool assertions go away.

The second still looks preferable to me for that reason: it preserves what the existing test was written to protect. But that test's title suggests the drop was a deliberate cross-provider decision (the fixture is OpenAI `reasoningEncryptedContent`, not Anthropic), so I don't want to repurpose it without a maintainer's call.

One more thing worth flagging: the same guard also feeds the OpenAI path at line 299 ("restores OpenAI encrypted reasoning metadata"), so relaxing it is not Anthropic-scoped.

Still happy to do this, just want the direction confirmed first given the test coupling. Same question on `dev` vs `v2` as above.

I hit this on NixOS+WSL2 and tracked down the root cause. Note Opus helped me debug this so take that as you will. It's an ELF layout problem in the built binary, and the WSL2 kernel is stricter about it than mainline.

opencode --version
1.18.4

uname -r
6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2

nix --version
nix (Nix) 2.34.8

nixos-version
26.11.20260729.0954f7e (Zokor)

## Root cause

The crash is in `ld.so`, before any opencode code runs:

    .opencode-wrapp[1737907]: segfault at 6510e40 ip 00007603d54370e8 error 6
      in ld-linux-x86-64.so.2

    SIGSEGV {si_signo=SIGSEGV, si_code=SEGV_MAPERR, si_addr=0x6510e40}

That address is not arbitrary. It's a copy relocation target:

    $ readelf -r bin/.opencode-wrapped | grep COPY
    000006510e40  R_X86_64_COPY  stderr@GLIBC_2.2.5 + 0
    000006510e20  R_X86_64_COPY  environ@GLIBC_2.2.5 + 0
    000006510e28  R_X86_64_COPY  stdout@GLIBC_2.2.5 + 0

The binary's `PT_LOAD` segments are not in ascending `p_vaddr` order — the 85MB
`.bun` payload segment is emitted first:

    $ readelf -lW bin/.opencode-wrapped | awk '/LOAD/{print $3, $6}'
    0x0000000006511000 0x515f000   <-- .bun payload, first
    0x00000000001ff000 0x001000
    0x0000000000200000 0x2806560
    0x0000000002b20c00 0x386f210
    0x0000000006390e10 0x180038    <-- RW/bss, ends at 0x6510e48

The ELF spec requires `PT_LOAD` entries to be sorted by `p_vaddr`, and the
kernel's ELF loader relies on that to size the `.bss` mapping. With the
ordering wrong, the final page of `.bss` never gets mapped — and the three
copy relocations above land in exactly that page. `ld.so` faults on the first
one it writes.

## Why it's WSL2-specific

Mainline kernels tolerate the bad ordering; the WSL2 kernel does not. That's
consistent with the package building and caching fine on Hydra while failing
on every WSL2 machine.

It also explains a detail worth knowing for anyone trying to debug this under
Nix: you cannot rebuild opencode locally on WSL2, because the build script's
own smoke test crashes:

    building opencode-linux-x64
    Running smoke test: dist/opencode-linux-x64/bin/opencode --version
    Smoke test failed for opencode-linux-x64: ShellError: Failed with exit code 139

That `dist/` binary is pre-patchelf, straight out of `bun build --compile`, so
the malformed layout is present the moment the executable is compiled — it is
not introduced by any later Nix-side patching. Since the install-script binary
reportedly works on WSL2, the released artifacts appear to have a correct
segment order, which suggests this comes from how the binary is compiled in
this build rather than from anything inherent to the released build. Running
the `readelf -lW` command above against a release binary and a locally
compiled one would confirm that directly.

## Fix / workaround

Rewriting the interpreter to the value it already has is semantically a no-op,
but it forces patchelf to regenerate the program header table, which emits the
segments correctly sorted:

    patchelf --set-interpreter "$(patchelf --print-interpreter FILE)" FILE

(Thanks @sonowz!)

After that the `.bun` segment moves from first to last and the binary starts.
Verified on 1.18.4 and reproduced identically on 1.18.11 (byte-identical
segment addresses, so version bumps alone won't help).

For nixpkgs users, this has to post-process the cached build rather than use
`overrideAttrs`, since any override triggers the local rebuild that fails the
smoke test above. The nixpkgs wrapper also hardcodes the original store path,
so the fixed inner binary needs a fresh wrapper.

A couple of questions for anyone who knows the build better than I do: is
emitting sorted program headers something that can be controlled at compile
time here, or is the post-hoc rewrite the practical route? And would a segment
ordering check be worth adding to the release pipeline? The existing smoke test
does catch this, but only on a kernel strict enough to fault, so it passes CI
and surfaces later on WSL2. 

Happy

I independently hit the same issue and did extensive debugging. Here are detailed findings that may help track down the root cause.

**Environment:** OpenCode 1.17.9 · Codex CLI 0.146.0 · Windows 11 Enterprise · ChatGPT Business, EU data residency · OAuth auth

**Key finding:** Codex CLI succeeds with the exact same account and credentials. Tested via:
```
echo "Say OK" | codex exec -m "gpt-5.5" --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
# → OK

echo "Say OK" | codex exec -m "gpt-5.6-sol" --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
# → OK

opencode run --model "openai/gpt-5.5" --agent plan "Say OK"
# → data_residency_mismatch
```

**Model availability (OpenCode, EU account):**

| Status | Models |
|--------|--------|
| Works | `gpt-5.4-mini`, `gpt-5.4-mini-fast` |
| `data_residency_mismatch` | `gpt-5.4`, `gpt-5.5`, `gpt-5.6-luna`, `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.6-terra` and `-fast`/`-pro` variants |
| Not supported on Codex plan | `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`, `gpt-5.5-pro`, `gpt-5.6`, `gpt-5.6-pro` |

**Request comparison — OpenCode vs Codex CLI:**

Both send identical:
- Endpoint: `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`
- Body: `model: "gpt-5.5"`, `store: false`, `stream: true`, `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`
- Auth: same OAuth token with same JWT claims (`chatgpt_data_residency: "eu"`, `chatgpt_compute_residency: "eu"`)
- Same `ChatGPT-Account-Id` header

**What I tried via OpenCode plugin (all confirmed active via fetch interception logs):**

| Override | Result |
|----------|--------|
| `originator: codex_cli_rs` (fetch-level, after built-in hook) | Still fails |
| `x-openai-internal-codex-residency: us` | Still fails |
| `x-openai-product-sku: codex` | Still fails |
| All three combined | Still fails |
| `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_WEBSOCKETS=true` | Still fails |

The OpenAI backend rejects the request regardless of header values. The exemption for Codex CLI appears to be based on something beyond HTTP headers — possibly transport-level (Rust reqwest vs Bun fetch), Cloudflare routing, or server-side client classification.

PR #15844 attempted to add the residency header but even with it applied, the issue persists.

**Update:** oh-my-pi had the exact same issue and already fixed it — [can1357/oh-my-pi#7198](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/issues/7198).

Root cause confirmed: **OpenAI backend enforces data residency on HTTP/SSE transport but not on WebSocket.** Their V2 compaction was using direct `fetch()` (SSE) to `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`, while the official Codex CLI uses WebSocket-first transport. Switching to WebSocket resolved the issue.

The fix was in [can1357/oh-my-pi#7202](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/pull/7202) — routing requests through the WebSocket-capable provider session instead of direct SSE fetch.

OpenCode has `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_WEBSOCKETS` support in the Codex plugin, but it does not seem to cover all request paths (I tested with the env var enabled and it still failed — possibly title generation or other requests still go through HTTP).

Confirmed this still reproduces on **v1.18.9**. I am adding this as a non-duplicate data point because the failure can occur with only a very small ordering mismatch.

### Observed invariant violation

Across three persisted occurrences:

- the user row's stored `time.created` preceded its first assistant by **31–44 ms**;
- nevertheless, the first assistant ID sorted lexicographically *before* its user parent ID;
- the assistant finished with `finish: "stop"` and had no tool calls;
- **4–7 ms** after that terminal completion, `SessionPrompt.runLoop()` created a second terminal assistant with the same `parentID`.

So the server-side durable timestamp and the lexical ID order disagreed. The next loop iteration misses its exit condition solely because of:

```ts
lastUser.id < lastAssistant.id
```

### Minimal local validation

I changed only the exit predicate in `packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts`:

```diff
- lastUser.id < lastAssistant.id
+ lastAssistant.parentID === lastUser.id
```

`parentID` is the actual turn-ownership invariant, so it also handles equal timestamps and client/server clock differences without relying on an ordering heuristic.

I added a regression test that seeds a completed assistant whose ID sorts before its user parent (`msg_a` vs `msg_z`) and verifies that `prompt.loop()` exits without starting another model request.

Validation on the current source checkout:

```text
bun test test/session/prompt.test.ts
57 pass, 1 skip, 0 fail

bun typecheck
passed
```

This is the same one-line fix proposed in the issue, with a concrete current-version reproduction and regression coverage.

## Suggestion: pass through DeepSeek's official `/v1/responses` instead of converting from chat/completions

First of all, thanks for the work on #40210 — much appreciated. I'd like to suggest a simpler and more robust direction for DeepSeek V4 Flash on the Go service: **just proxy the request through to DeepSeek's official `/v1/responses` endpoint**, the same way GPT-5.x models are already handled natively.

DeepSeek's official API has natively supported the Responses API for `deepseek-v4-flash` since the 0731 checkpoint. I verified this directly:

- `POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/responses` with `model: deepseek-v4-flash` works — including **tools** (`{"type":"web_search"}` is accepted and returns proper `web_search_call` output items).

The chat-completions → Responses conversion layer on the Go service, on the other hand, is currently breaking requests in at least three independent ways for this model:

1. **Missing lifecycle events** (`response.created`, `response.output_item.added`, `response.content_part.added`, `response.output_item.done`) — already tracked in #40210. Codex-style clients hang or fail without them.
2. **`web_search` tool declaration → HTTP 400**: if the request's `tools` array contains `{"type":"web_search"}` at any position, the upstream returns `Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: tools[N].function: missing field 'name'` (N varies with tool ordering). The deserializer seems to treat unknown tool types as malformed function tools. Verified with both Codex CLI and a plain curl against `opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/responses`; the identical request succeeds against DeepSeek's official endpoint.
3. **`reasoning_content` dropped across tool-call turns** in thinking mode (the #35689 / #25758 / #24722 / #28974 family) — which makes DeepSeek reject subsequent turns or silently stop mid-task.

All three issues disappear if requests for `deepseek-v4-flash` are forwarded verbatim to the official Responses upstream instead of being parsed/rebuilt/converted by the gateway. Since the official endpoint already supports everything the Responses protocol needs (including native web search), a passthrough would also fix the Codex/cc-switch use case end-to-end.

Would it be possible to route DeepSeek models on `/v1/responses` directly to `api.deepseek.com/v1/responses`?
